summary: Food must be the size of an egg to pass on the tumah of food. Things stuck to the meat, like skin, bones, and gravy, join with the meat to make that size, but not to make the kezayis of a neveilah.

chunks.en: The skin, and the gravy,
chunks.st: the attached hide, even if it is not fit for consumption, joins together with the meat to constitute an egg-bulk. And the same is true of the congealed gravy attached to the meat, although it is not eaten;

chunks.en: and the spices, and the leftover meat on the skin,
chunks.st: and likewise the spices added to flavor the meat, although they are not eaten; and the meat residue attached to the hide after flaying;

words.note: Bits of meat stuck to the skin.

chunks.en: and the bones, and the sinews,
chunks.st: and the bones; and the tendons;

chunks.en: and the horns, and the hooves,
chunks.st: and the lower section of the horns, which remains attached to the flesh when the rest of the horn is removed; and the upper section of the hooves, which remains attached to the flesh when the rest of the hoof is removed.

chunks.en: join together to make the tumah of food,
chunks.explain: Together with the meat, they make an egg's size.
chunks.st: All these items join together with the meat to constitute the requisite egg-bulk to impart the impurity of food.
chunks.stMore: Although if any of them was an egg-bulk they would not impart impurity of food, when attached to the meat they complete the measure.

chunks.en: but not the tumah of a neveilah.
chunks.st: But they do not join together to constitute the measure of an olive-bulk required to impart the impurity of animal carcasses.

chunks.en: Like this:

chunks.st: one who slaughters a non-kosher animal for a gentile and the animal is still twitching and comes into contact with a source of impurity, the animal becomes impure with impurity of food and

chunks.en: it makes things tamei with the tumah of food,
chunks.st: imparts impurity of food to other food,

chunks.en: but not with the tumah of a neveilah,
chunks.st: but does not impart impurity of animal carcasses

chunks.en: until it dies or until
chunks.st: until it dies, or

chunks.en: its head is cut off.
chunks.st: until one severs its head.

chunks.en: The Torah included more things for the tumah of food than
chunks.st: The mishna summarizes: The Torah included certain items to impart impurity of food

chunks.en: it included for the tumah of a neveilah.
chunks.st: beyond those which it included to impart impurity of animal carcasses.

chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says: With regard to

chunks.en: Meat bits that were gathered together,

chunks.he: אִם יֶשׁ בּוֹ כַזַּיִת בְּמָקוֹם אֶחָד,
chunks.en: if there is a kezayis of it in one place,
chunks.st: if there is an olive-bulk of it in one place it imparts impurity of an animal carcass, and one who contracts impurity from it and then eats consecrated foods or enters the Temple is

chunks.en: one is liable for it.
chunks.st: liable to receive karet.
chunks.stMore: By collecting it in one place, the person indicates that he considers it as meat.

stIntro: All foods that became ritually impure through contact with a source of impurity transmit impurity to other food and liquids only if the impure foods measure an egg-bulk. In that regard, the Sages ruled that even if a piece of meat itself is less than an egg-bulk,

summary: For some animals, the skin counts like the meat for tumah, like a pig's skin and the soft skin of young animals. Once they are tanned, they are tahor, except for a person's skin.

chunks.en: These are the ones whose skin counts like their meat:
chunks.st: These are the entities whose skin has the same halakhic status as their flesh:

chunks.en: The skin of a person,
chunks.st: The skin of a dead person, which imparts impurity like his flesh;

chunks.en: and the skin of a pig raised among people.
chunks.st: and the skin of a domesticated pig, which is soft and eaten by gentiles, and imparts the impurity of an animal carcass like its flesh.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yosei says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.en: Even the skin of a wild pig.
chunks.st: Even the skin of a wild boar has the same status.

chunks.en: And the skin of a young camel's hump,
chunks.st: And the halakhic status of the skin of all of the following animals is also like that of their flesh: The skin of the hump of a young camel that did not yet toughen;

chunks.en: and the skin of a young calf's head,
chunks.st: and the skin of the head of a young calf;

chunks.en: and the skin of the hooves,
chunks.st: and the hide of the hooves;

chunks.en: and the skin of a private place,
chunks.st: and the skin of the womb;

chunks.en: and the skin of an unborn calf,
chunks.st: and the skin of an animal fetus in the womb of a slaughtered animal;

chunks.en: and the skin under the tail,
chunks.st: and the skin beneath the tail of a ewe;

chunks.en: and the skin of the anakah, the ko'ach, the leta'ah, and the chomet.
chunks.explain: Four kinds of small creeping animals, like lizards.
chunks.st: and the skin of the gecko [anaka], and the desert monitor [ko’aḥ], and the lizard [leta’a], and the skink [ḥomet], four of the eight creeping animals that impart ritual impurity after death.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehudah says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says: The halakhic status of the skin of

chunks.en: The leta'ah is like the weasel.
chunks.explain: Its skin does not count like its meat.
chunks.st: the lizard is like that of the skin of the weasel and is not like that of its flesh.

chunks.en: And all of them, if he tanned them, or walked
chunks.st: And with regard to all of these skins, in a case where one tanned them or spread them on the ground and

chunks.en: on them long enough to tan them,
chunks.st: trod upon them for the period of time required for tanning, they are no longer classified as flesh and are

chunks.en: are tahor, except for the skin of a person.
chunks.st: ritually pure, except for the skin of a person, which maintains the status of flesh.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri says: All

chunks.en: The eight sheratzim have skins.
chunks.explain: Sheratzim are small creeping animals that make things tamei.
chunks.st: eight creeping animals enumerated in the Torah have skins whose halakhic status is not that of flesh.

summary: While an animal is being skinned, the skin still counts as connected to the meat for tumah until enough of it is taken off, depending on what he is making from the skin.

chunks.en: Someone who skins a farm animal or a wild animal,
chunks.st: Nevertheless, in the case of one who flays either a domesticated animal or an undomesticated animal;

chunks.en: a tahor one or a tamei one,
chunks.st: a ritually pure animal that was slaughtered properly and afterward came in contact with impurity, e.g., the one flaying it is impure, or a ritually impure unslaughtered carcass;

chunks.en: a small one or a big one:
chunks.st: a small animal, e.g., sheep, or a large animal, e.g., cattle;
chunks.stMore: and even after flaying the animal’s hide is still partially attached to the flesh, the hide’s halakhic status remains that of flesh in some circumstances.

chunks.en: for a rug, until he skins a handful.
chunks.st: These circumstances are: If he is flaying the animal for the purpose of using the hide as a carpet, a tablecloth, or to drape over a couch, in which case he would cut the hide along the length of the animal from head to tail and then remove the hide from both sides, its halakhic status remains that of flesh until he has flayed the measure of grasping the hide, i.e., two handbreadths.

chunks.en: For a leather jug, until he skins the chest.
chunks.st: And if he is flaying the animal for the purpose of crafting a leather jug, in which case he cuts a circle near the animal’s neck and removes the hide in a downward movement, its halakhic status remains that of flesh until he flays the animal’s entire breast.

chunks.en: If he skins it starting from the legs, all of it is connected for tumah,
chunks.st: In the case of one who seeks to fashion a jug and begins flaying from the legs, until he removes the animal’s hide in its entirety, the entire hide is considered as having a connection with the flesh and its halakhic status remains that of flesh with regard to impurity, i.e., with regard

words.en: one who starts from the legs

chunks.en: to become tamei and to make tamei.
chunks.st: to becoming impure and with regard to imparting impurity. If one removed the entire hide except for

chunks.en: The skin on the neck:
chunks.st: the hide over the neck,

chunks.en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri says:

chunks.en: It is not connected.
chunks.st: It is not considered to have a connection to the flesh,

chunks.en: And the Sages say:
chunks.st: and the Rabbis say: It is considered to have a

chunks.en: It is connected until he skins all of it.
chunks.st: connection to the flesh until he removes the animal’s hide in its entirety, including the neck.

stIntro: The halakhic status of the hide of an animal after it was flayed is no longer like its flesh in terms of becoming impure and imparting impurity.

summary: If a neveilah's skin has a kezayis of meat on it, touching a strand or hair of it makes a person tamei. Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva argue about two half-kezaysim of meat on the skin.

chunks.en: A skin that has a kezayis of meat on it:
chunks.st: In the case of a hide of an unslaughtered carcass upon which there is an olive-bulk of flesh,

chunks.en: someone who touches a strand of meat coming out of it,
chunks.st: one who touches a strand of flesh emerging from the flesh

chunks.en: or a hair on the other side of it,
chunks.st: or a hair that is on the side of the hide opposite the flesh

chunks.en: is tamei.
chunks.st: is ritually impure.
chunks.stMore: Although he did not touch an olive-bulk of the flesh, he is rendered impure with the impurity of an unslaughtered carcass. The reason is that the strand of flesh has the same status as the flesh itself, and the hair is considered protection to the flesh, which also has the same status as the flesh with regard to one who touches it.

chunks.en: If there were two half-kezaysim on it,
chunks.st: If upon the hide there were two half olive-bulks, the hide

chunks.en: it makes tamei by carrying, but not by touching.
chunks.st: imparts the impurity of an unslaughtered carcass by means of carrying, because one moves them together, but not by means of contact with the flesh, because one touches them separately;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Yishmael says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Yishmael.

chunks.en: Rabbi Akiva says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Akiva says: The hide does not impart impurity,

chunks.en: Not by touching and not by carrying.
chunks.st: neither by means of contact nor by means of carrying.

chunks.en: And Rabbi Akiva agrees about two half-kezaysim
chunks.st: And Rabbi Akiva concedes in the case of

chunks.en: that he stuck on a stick and moved,
chunks.st: two half olive-bulks where one skewered them with a wood chip and moved them

chunks.en: that he is tamei.
chunks.st: that he is impure.

chunks.he: וּמִפְּנֵי מָה רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא מְטַהֵר בָּעוֹר,
chunks.en: So why does Rabbi Akiva say he is tahor with the skin?
chunks.st: And for what reason does Rabbi Akiva deem one ritually pure in a case where he moved both half olive-bulks with the hide, as in that case, too, he moved them together?

chunks.en: Because the skin cancels them.
chunks.explain: The skin keeps the two halves apart.
chunks.st: It is because the hide separates between them and nullifies them.

summary: A thigh bone of a dead person or of a korban makes tamei even when closed. A thigh bone of a neveilah or a sheretz makes tamei only if it has a hole, because the marrow inside is what makes tamei.

chunks.en: The thigh bone of a dead person, or the thigh bone of a korban,
chunks.st: With regard to the thigh bone of a human corpse, and the thigh bone of a sacrificial animal
chunks.stMore: that was rendered unfit as piggul, i.e., an offering that was sacrificed with the intent to consume it after its designated time, or notar, i.e., part of an offering left over after the time allotted for its consumption,

chunks.he: הַנּוֹגֵעַ בָּהֶן, בֵּין סְתוּמִים בֵּין נְקוּבִים, טָמֵא.
chunks.en: someone who touches them, whether they are closed or have a hole, is tamei.
chunks.st: whether these thigh bones were sealed and there was no access to the marrow, or whether they were perforated and there was access to the marrow, one who touches them is ritually impure.
chunks.stMore: The reason is that a piece of bone of a corpse the size of a barley grain imparts impurity, and the bone of a sacrificial animal that was disqualified in this manner imparts impurity by rabbinic decree via contact.

chunks.en: The thigh bone of a neveilah or the thigh bone of a sheretz:
chunks.st: With regard to the thigh bone of an unslaughtered carcass and the thigh bone of a creeping animal,

chunks.en: someone who touches them when they are closed
chunks.st: one who touches them when they are sealed remains

chunks.en: stays tahor. If it has any hole at all,
chunks.st: ritually pure. If one of these thigh bones was perforated at all,

chunks.en: it makes tamei by touching.
chunks.st: it imparts impurity via contact,
chunks.stMore: as in that case contact with the bone is tantamount to contact with the marrow.

chunks.en: How do we know that also by carrying?
chunks.st: From where is it derived that even with regard to impurity transmitted via carrying there is a distinction between sealed and perforated thigh bones?

chunks.en: The pasuk says (Vayikra 11):
chunks.st: It is derived from a verse, as the verse states: “

chunks.en: "the one who touches" and "the one who carries."
chunks.st: One who touches the carcass thereof shall be impure until the evening; and one who carries the carcass thereof shall be impure until the evening” (Leviticus 11:39–40), indicating:

chunks.en: What comes under the rule of touching
chunks.st: That which enters the category of impurity via contact,

chunks.en: comes under the rule of carrying.
chunks.st: enters the category of impurity via carrying;

chunks.en: What does not come under the rule of touching
chunks.st: that which does not enter the category of impurity via contact,

chunks.en: does not come under the rule of carrying.
chunks.st: does not enter the category of impurity via carrying.

summary: A sheretz's egg with a chick growing inside is tahor while closed, but tamei once it has a hole. The mishnah also talks about a mouse that is half flesh and half earth.

chunks.en: An egg of a sheretz with a baby forming inside
chunks.st: The egg of a creeping animal in which tissue of an embryo developed and one who comes into contact with the egg are

chunks.en: is tahor. If it got any hole at all,
chunks.st: ritually pure, as the impure creeping animal is hermetically sealed. But if one perforated the egg with a hole of any size, one who comes in contact with the egg is

chunks.he: טְמֵאָה. עַכְבָּר שֶׁחֶצְיוֹ בָשָׂר וְחֶצְיוֹ אֲדָמָה,
chunks.en: it is tamei. A mouse that is half flesh and half earth:
chunks.explain: People thought some mice grew out of the ground.
chunks.st: ritually impure. In the case of a mouse that grows from the ground and is half-flesh half-earth,

chunks.en: someone who touches the flesh
chunks.st: one who touches the half that is flesh is

chunks.en: is tamei. If he touches the earth,
chunks.st: impure; one who touches the half that is earth is

chunks.en: he is tahor. Rabbi Yehudah says:
chunks.st: pure. Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.he: אַף הַנּוֹגֵעַ בָּאֲדָמָה שֶׁכְּנֶגֶד הַבָּשָׂר, טָמֵא:
chunks.en: Even someone who touches the earth next to the flesh is tamei.
chunks.st: Even one who touches the half that is earth where it is adjacent to the flesh is ritually impure.

summary: A limb or meat that is partly cut and hanging from an animal can get the tumah of food once it is made wet. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon argue about what happens when the animal is shechted or dies.

chunks.en: A limb or meat hanging loose from an animal
chunks.st: The limb of an animal, with flesh, sinews, and bones, and the flesh of an animal, that were partially severed and remain hanging from the animal
chunks.stMore: do not have the halakhic status of a limb severed from a living animal, which imparts impurity like an unslaughtered carcass, or of flesh severed from a living animal, which is ritually pure, respectively. If one had intent to eat the limb or the flesh, the limb or flesh becomes impure if it comes in contact with a source of impurity, and they

chunks.en: make things tamei with the tumah of food while still in their place,
chunks.st: impart impurity as food to other foods and liquids, although they remain in their place attached to the animal.

chunks.en: and they need to be made ready.
chunks.explain: Made wet by certain liquids, so they can become tamei.
chunks.st: But in order for them to become impure, they need to be rendered susceptible to impurity through contact with one of the seven liquids that facilitate susceptibility. If

chunks.en: If the animal was shechted,
chunks.st: the animal was slaughtered,
chunks.stMore: although this act of slaughter does not render it permitted for consumption by a Jew (see 73b), the limb and the flesh

chunks.en: they were made ready by its blood.
chunks.st: were thereby rendered susceptible to impurity by coming in contact with the blood of the slaughtered animal, as blood is one of the seven liquids;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Shimon says:

chunks.en: They were not made ready.
chunks.st: They were not rendered susceptible to impurity through the animal’s own blood;
chunks.stMore: they are rendered susceptible only once they have been wet with another liquid. If

chunks.en: If the animal died,
chunks.st: the animal died without slaughter,

chunks.en: the meat needs to be made ready.
chunks.st: the hanging flesh needs to be rendered susceptible to impurity in order to become impure,
chunks.stMore: as its halakhic status is that of flesh severed from a living animal, which is ritually pure and does not have the status of an unslaughtered carcass.

chunks.he: הָאֵבָר מְטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבָר מִן הַחַי
chunks.en: The limb makes tamei as a limb from a living animal,
chunks.st: The hanging limb imparts impurity as a limb severed from a living animal

chunks.en: but it does not make tamei as a limb of a neveilah.
chunks.st: but does not impart impurity as the limb of an unslaughtered carcass;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: And Rabbi Shimon says it is tahor.
chunks.st: And Rabbi Shimon deems the limb ritually pure.

summary: A limb or flesh hanging loose from a living person is tahor. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon argue about the limb after the person dies.

chunks.en: A limb or flesh hanging loose from a person
chunks.st: The limb and the flesh of a person that were partially severed and remain hanging from a person

chunks.en: are tahor. If the person died,
chunks.st: are ritually pure, although there is no potential for healing. If the person died,

chunks.en: the flesh is tahor.
chunks.st: the hanging flesh is ritually pure, as its halakhic status is that of flesh severed from a living person.

chunks.he: הָאֵבָר מְטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבָר מִן הַחַי
chunks.en: The limb makes tamei as a limb from the living,
chunks.st: The hanging limb imparts impurity as a limb severed from the living

chunks.he: וְאֵינוֹ מְטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבָר מִן הַמֵּת,
chunks.en: but it does not make tamei as a limb from the dead.
chunks.st: and does not impart impurity as a limb from a corpse;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: And Rabbi Shimon says it is tahor.
chunks.st: And Rabbi Shimon deems the flesh and the limb ritually pure.
